utterances.text: You describe it. You're not blamed for inventing. Mr. Misetic disagrees with your analysis, which is he doesn't disagree because you invented but because he thinks it's wrong. So there's no need to defend yourself. Just answer the questions, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, if we could go to Article 10, which is, I believe, page 5. If we scroll to the bottom it says: "The military police perform jobs and tasks relating to the: 1, protection of life and personal security of military personnel ..." If we can go to the next page, please. "Prevention and uncovering of crimes, identification and arrest of perpetrators of crimes, ... Safety of military traffic ... security of protected features ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now you raise this point about how Mr. Lausic complained to Mr. Susak, and my understanding of your answer was that somehow he was trying to -- use Mr. Susak to influence General Gotovina so he could get those troops back.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I pointed out, the report by General Lausic addressed the use of the military police all over Croatia, i.e., I have not -- there is no mention specifically of the Split Military District in that document, and that Mr. Lausic reports to Mr. Susak is quite logical because Mr. Lausic is the chief of the military police administration at the Ministry of Defence. So his next superior is Mr. Susak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But that whole issue arose in the context of me asking you a question of whether Mr. Lausic could issue an order to General Gotovina, and you answered not directly, meaning indirectly, and then you said, for example, he contacted Minister Susak, and then subsequently General Lausic issued an order, and then General Gotovina issued an order. And implicit, as I understood it - and you correct me if I'm wrong - implicit in your answer was that he could indirectly issue an order by appealing to the Ministry of Defence, and then somehow from that chain it would get to General Gotovina. Was that your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My conclusion is that the commander -- the chief of the military police administration reports to the Minister of Defence, and then it is up to the minister of Defence to do or to act upon the reporting he receives of the chief of the military police administration and to give instructions to the chief of the Main Staff who then gives instructions to his subordinates. And I only gave the example to answer your question in relation to General Lausic issuing orders to General Gotovina or not, but I didn't suggest or that -- it was an issue of Mr. Susak using his influence over General Gotovina, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if I could turn your attention to subpart 9 in Article 10. It says: "Participation in carrying out combat tasks on the front line, pursuant to orders by the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia." Now, do you see that the reason Mr. Lausic appealed to Minister Susak first is because it's Minister Susak's order that orders the military police combat units to go participate in combat, particularly here in the Split Military District, and that General Lausic needed his superior's authorisation to then remove them the next day.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have quoted a number of orders from the commander of the Split Military District in relation to subordination as well as the use of elements of the 72nd Military Police Battalion as well as reports on the use of elements of the 73rd Military Police Battalion during Storm for combat operations, and there is no systematic reference to an order by or an authorisation given by Mr. Susak. It would be the easiest if you see these orders. I think, for example --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again I'm focussed on the order of the 9th which is an order that you raised. So without going into now a long discussion about what you didn't find, I'm asking you specifically in the context of you -- you raising the point that Mr. Lausic wrote to Minister Susak about the combat units, isn't it a fact at that Mr. Lausic, under the existing regulations, needed the authorisation of the Minister Of Defence under Article 10, subpart 9, to remove those units from combat activity?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be precise, General Lausic reports regularly to Minister Susak, but it is correct that the order he issues on the 10th of August refers to a decision of the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So now, in this situation, you would agree with me, I hope that we're in a situation where the minister of defence is authorised alone in the rules to authorise use of combat units of the military police, where he revokes that authorisation through an order of the chief of the military police administration. General Gotovina has no authority to overrule General Lausic or the Minister Of Defence; does he?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically, he hasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Theoretically and in practice, right? You have never seen in practice General Gotovina overriding an order of the Minister Of Defence; have you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I have seen -- that is another aspect, but I have seen that he in direct contact with Minister Susak, whereas I would expect him to -- discussing operational matters, where would I would expect him to discuss these matters with the chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So the answer is no, you haven't seen him overriding an answer of the Minister Of Defence, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You haven't seen him overriding an order of the chief of the military police administration, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean an order from the chief military police administration to him or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or an order of the chief military police administration to a military police unit of the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First of all, let's take the second, which an order of the chief of the military police administration to the 72nd MP Battalion.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not come across such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the first part of your initial request for clarification, he didn't override an order from Mr. Lausic to him because there is no such order from Mr. Lausic to General Gotovina, correct? Meaning ordering General Gotovina to do something, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 10th of August order we discussed, which goes from General Lausic to the military police battalions puts the Military District Commanders for information, so it is not a direct order to Gotovina, but because it concerns General Gotovina's units, as well as the units ever other Military District Commanders, he is informed of -- of General Lausic's order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to understand, because apparently there is an -- some fear to use the wrong words. Decisions for the engagement - and I add to that then for disengagement as well - of police forces of the military police. In combat operations on the front line are the competence of the minister of defence to decide is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what Article 9 says, Mr. President, in general terms. But he is not going to get involved with each and every decision once he has given that authorisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I mean the level of detail with which the orders deal with the engagement or disagreement is another matter. But is it clear that that's the exclusive competence of the Minister Of Justice. To that extent, if Mr. Gotovina is informed about that, he just has to accept that as a decision. I mean, whether he tries behind the scenes to -- whatever -- but in formal terms, that is a decision binding upon him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you mean -- yeah, the disengagement, that's often, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I that I was the issue you wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now with respect to these other tasks that are enumerated in Article 10, these are -- these are not -- and this may be an issue of language, so bear with me here. These are not daily operational tasks. These are permanent tasks of the military police. These are the constant duties of the military police that don't change from day to day, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 9, Your Honour, uses the language regular military police tasks. For me the tasks that are enumerated in Article 9 are regular military police tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you mean enumerated in Article 10, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, Article 10 of P880.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now my question next question because the orders of General Lausic beginning on the 3rd, including his summary of -- in September of 1995 and his year 1995 assessment from January of 1996, use the phrase "daily operational command." And what I'd like first to establish with you is these tasks are what we would call the constant duties of the military police, correct? They don't change from day to day?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: These tasks can change because there may not everyday, for example, a requirement to protect a feature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let try to get the question clear. The tasks in the abstract will be the same everyday, but require concrete decisions as to what features, persons, and areas would be in need of security, what crimes are there to be uncovered, et cetera. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, will you agree with me that, for example, in paragraph 2, the crime police of the military police administration at the level of the 72nd MP Battalion, they had a vertical line that went and reported, for example, on the progress of any criminal investigation in the military police, the daily reporting on the progress of the investigation went to the military police administration, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm thinking now of the document we discussed in relation to the illegal occupation of apartments in Split where also the operational commander was kept informed of the progress of an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, once again you're giving what you know to be the -- the exception to the rule. What I'm asking you is give me the general practice. General practice is the crime investigation section of the 72nd MP Battalion on a daily basis reports to the MP administration, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to the professional line. Now, whether the example I gave is an exception or not, I -- I don't share that conclusion with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay, how many other such situations did you find, 10, 20, 50?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would need time to review my report. I cannot say that here immediately. But I don't see anything irregular in the document we discussed, I mean the document about the illegal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's another matter. Whether it's routinely done or whether it is irregular, of course, is not the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said whether the example you gave is an exception or not, you don't share that conclusion. At this moment, if there's any reason for you that -- to tell us that it was not an exception which was more or less suggested by Mr. Misetic, please, on the basis of perhaps a further analysis, inform us about that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, while we have this document on the screen, Mr. Registrar, if we could turn to Article 15 to address a matter that Mr. Theunens raised this morning, which is page 7, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now you said that it wasn't part of the regular duties of the military police on monitoring discipline.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Theunens is right. It's not what you said. Could you please literally quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will quote him then. Let's just take them through Article 15, Article 15, subparts 2, 3, and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "While performing their tasks, the members of the military police apply the following powers," number 2 is identification. And it says: "It is applied for the purpose of verifying the identity of persons in all cases when identity information can be used for uncovering crimes and identifying the perpetrators uncovering perpetrators of military discipline and misdemeanours." And if we go to subpart 3, please. It talks about the reporting by the military police and it says: "Members of the military police submit a disciplinary report against military personnel who violate military discipline and a criminal report against persons who commit a crime that falls within the jurisdiction of a military court." Subpart 4 says: "Bringing in ..." talks about ability to bring perpetrators in. "Individuals -- sorry members it says: Members of the military police bring in military personnel when ..." And then amongst other things "...military personnel and civilians in the service of the RH armed forces because of violations of military discipline. Individuals are brought in." And then part 3 is: "If the person was caught in an act of serious violation of military discipline and the circumstances indicate that the violation of military discipline would continue." So it's clear that the duties of the military police include identifying a violator of military discipline, filing a report against a violator of military discipline. And in situations where it is a serious violation concerning ongoing violations of military discipline, they bring that person in, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are duties of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And one of the things that a commander is entitled to reply on, wouldn't you agree, is that the military police, in addition to uncovering crime, is also filing those reports with the appropriate commanders of the units of the violator of military discipline so that commander with then act and issue military discipline against that violator, correct? It is one of the tools of a commander.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, and we remember that we discussed the report on a traffic violation by a member of the 7th Guards Brigade at a time when the 7th Guards Brigade was subordinated to the Split Military District, whereby General Gotovina forwarded the report on the traffic violation that had been compiled by the 72nd Military Police Battalion to the commander of the 7th Guards Brigade and invited him to take disciplinary measures in order to act against the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you -- you want to raise that issue as well, so while I'm here and while we're in this context, let's talk about that specific incident. You claimed in direct examination that that was an exercise of powers under Article 26. My question to you is: If the 7th Guards Brigade is subordinated to the Split Military District when this traffic violation occurred, why didn't the military police just directly send the report to General Korade of the 7th Guards Brigade to take discipline? Why does it have to go from the military police up to the commander of the Split Military District then down to the 7th Guards Brigade commander if they're all in the same Military District?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, because Article -- I mean, it's an application of Article 26. The violation has been observed in the zone of responsibility of the Split Military District. The 72nd Military Police Battalion is the military police battalion of the Split Military District. If we -- in accordance with Article 26, the 72nd Military Police Battalion, when they report the violation to General Gotovina, do not what measures General Gotovina will take.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on Article 26 General Gotovina can take measures himself, if he considers that it is it a serious violation. If General Gotovina considers that it is it not a serious matter, in accordance with Article 26 he then refers the matter to the commander of the 7th Guards Brigade. So I don't see anything irregular in -- in the fact that the 72nd Military Police Battalion reported the violation to General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again if I could get you focus back in on my question, okay. The 72nd MP Battalion knows that there's a traffic violation committed by the 7th Guards Brigade. Why didn't they just go straight to General Korade and ask him to take measures? Article 26 does not say only the Military District Commander has powers under Article 26, does it? It goes all the way down to at least the brigade level, in terms of the power of a commander to act. General Korade is a brigade commander. Why didn't the 72nd MP just go to General Korade who, in your theory, also has powers under Article 26 and just ask him to take measures against his own unit?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have given an answer to the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You'll help me along. I'm not sure what your answer is. Why didn't they go straight to General Korade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think your answer was there was nothing irregular. The question put to you by Mr. Misetic, however, is why not, to say so the easy way, was followed and why go up that high if the matter could have been dealt with at a lower level? If you know tell us if not, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me it an implementation of command and control at the most basic level. The forces or the members of the 7th Guards Brigade who commit the violation, commit the violation while they are subordinated to General Gotovina, and they commit the violation in Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The issue, I think, is whether every violation against discipline would have to be reported that high up. That, I think, is the question Mr. Misetic tries to seek an answer to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is not a question of that high up. And we can discuss that -- that aspect also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that is the aspect Mr. Misetic is asking you about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, General Gotovina takes several -- I mean, prior to Operation Storm, confirms or takes disciplinary measures on several issues or several violations and minor -- including also minor breaches of military discipline. That is how the procedure is applied. But the issue with the 7th and General Gotovina is actually that Split is not located in the zone of responsibility of the 7th Guards Brigade. So you have a -- an (alien) unit or members of an alien unit who commit a violation in Split at the time when this unit is subordinated to the Split Military District. The information I had did not allow me to conclude whether there is a command level between these members of the 7 Guards Brigade and the command of the Split Military District while these members of the 7 Guards Brigade are subordinated to General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your explanation is that it is due to the specific circumstances where the 7th Guards Brigade is subordinated but not usually within the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And also because the violation takes place in the zone of responsibility of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that causes this rather high-up procedure. There is not much higher up, is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think it is a question of just higher up. It's a question of following the structure and command and control as it is organised. That is, that the 72nd Military Police Battalion is a battalion of the Split Military District subordinated to General Gotovina, for the regular military police tasks. As we saw in Article 10 traffic control is a regular police task. So it wouldn't make sense at least from the military point of view to have the 72nd contact Colonel Korade directly in Varazdin for a matter that happened while the violators were actually subordinated to General Gotovina in a totally different area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have to follow up this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens let's forget it's the 7th Guard's Brigade. It's the 4th Guards Brigade. It's the 113th Home Guards. Are you saying that every soldier got into a traffic accident had his matter reported to General Gotovina for disciplinary measures to be taken? If we go through the statistics, do you expect that we're going to find General Gotovina issues disciplinary measures for traffic violations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the analysis of disciplinary violations we discussed during my examination and the document is P1121 where among the 15 measures that are ordered by General4k Gotovina in order to increase discipline, approximately ten directly deal with traffic violations and traffic accidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now -- Mr. Theunens let me stop you, okay. Because I need to you focus on the question. That is not an example of General Gotovina issuing discipline directly, is it? He is not issuing discipline against specific soldiers in that analysis, is he?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that was the first part of my answer, but it shows that General Gotovina considers traffic security and the behaviour of his subordinates in traffic as a -- a key matter. Because otherwise he himself would not issue these instructions. Coming back now to the traffic accidents well, or to whether Gotovina, yes or no, directly intervenes, well, it will depend on the nature of the accident. If it is just an accident as an accident, I don't expect him to intervene, but if there are serious disciplinary implications, i.e., drunk driving, several victims, and so on, and so on, whereby the person who investigates the matter decides that this is actually a serious violation of discipline --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I think we are losing ourselves at this moment in details. Your answer is clear. You say seriousness may play a role in whether it will be reported. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me explore it again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not saying that you shouldn't explore it. Let me also try to understand what we're dealing with at this moment. This was all triggered apparently by where you said would further explore the matter and not quote Mr. Theunens. I think Mr. Theunens testified that, although the military police has a specific task in disciplinary matters, that I think what he tried to explain to us, that this was not an exclusive task for the military police but that a commander had a -- had his own responsibility, and that's apparently what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not disputed. It's good to establish that, that -- then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As I said earlier this morning, I'm not averse if Mr. Theunens wants to go off on a tangent. At certain points I will follow him, but let's get to the issue of the 7th Guards Brigade because this is an issue highlighted in the direct examination, which is why I wanted to follow up with it anyway, but I'm prepared to follow this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, here is what I want to know based often your last answer now. Show me in the code of military discipline the principle that the military police, for example, can say well, this is one looks like it's a serious violation. More serious than other serious violations. I think this one should go up to General Gotovina, forget the intermediate commanders all up the chain, and this one should just straight to General Gotovina, because this one is a traffic violation that is it not blowing through a red light, this is drunk driving, and so this one needs to go all the way to the top. Where does it say that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is the question now whether the matter should go straight to General Gotovina or whether the chain of command should be followed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Straight to General Gotovina. Because that's your supposition that depending upon the seriousness of the disciplinary violation, it would go straight to General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honours. My answer in relation to the 7th Guards was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the 4th Guards and the natural units of the Split Military District. Let's establish this first. A member of a squad goes through a red light. The military police happens to get the report. They file a disciplinary report with whom in the Croatian disciplinary system?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the commander of -- of 4th Guards Brigade. But it's logical because the 4th Guards Brigade or the battalion commander of this squad leader. Why? Because the 4th Guards Brigade is a unit of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now let take it to the next step.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: A member of a squad of the 7th Guard's Brigade blows through a red light, and the military police is advised and files a disciplinary report with whom, and we're talking about 72nd military police?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all depends on the position of that squad. If that squad that is the only component of the 7th Guards Brigade subordinated to the Split Military District at a time it commits this traffic violation, then the report will go to the commander of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. Let take to what really happened, which is the entire 7th Guards Brigade with General Korade also is subordinated to the Split Military District. In that circumstance a member of a squad of the 7th Guards Brigade goes through a red light. Who does the 72nd MP Battalion file a disciplinary report with?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the example we discussed, it is brought to the attention of General Gotovina, and it is General Gotovina who sends it is to the commander of the 7 Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now you're talking the specific instances. I'm saying your understanding of the Code of Military Discipline is that it should have been sent to whom?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no reason to change my -- my view in relation to -- to the fact that what happened to the traffic violators of the 7th Guards Brigade is in line with the Code of Discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me consult to the ultimate point and see if you agree or disagree and we'll move on. The reason that it was sent to General Gotovina by the 72nd MP is that, as you said, normally if it were the 4th Guards Brigade, they would send it to General Krsticevic of the th Guards Brigade. Because the 7th Guards Brigade is not a situated in the Split Military District, it was sent to the Split MD command to be delivered to General Korade to take appropriate measures. It has nothing to do with the Article 26. It is the Split Military District basically acting as a postal service to deliver the measure to be department with by the appropriate commander. Isn't that all that happened there?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave my answer. I mean, I would wonder if it is so crystal clear as you put it, then I really wonder where the person who received the mail at the Split Military District Command had to bother General Gotovina with the matter. If it is like you explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- let's -- let's try to keep matters relatively simple. Mr. Misetic puts to you that sending the report to General Gotovina was not done because he was supposed to exercise any disciplinary power, but it was a matter of routing that this is the appropriate way of finally sending this report to the authority that was supposed to consider any disciplinary measures. That's what Mr. Misetic meant by a post office, apparently for formal reasons, to be there, not to -- not with an expectation that General Gotovina under those circumstances would do anything else than to send it to the command of the 7th Guards Brigade and not in an expectation to exercise disciplinary powers. That's what is put to you, and you're invited to tell us whether you agree with that or for what reasons you would disagree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not agree with that theory. Why? Because it is also -- it is General Gotovina who signs the document that is sent or at least whose name is on the document that is sent to the commander of the 7 Guards Brigade. If indeed the 72nd didn't know very well where to send it to and then just sent it to the Split Military District Command, and this was not in accordance with the procedures, then the appropriate person at the Split Military District Command would have sent the report back to the 72nd Military Police Battalion, and instructed them to send the document directly to General Korade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's why you say that this is not just a post office function. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And can you give me the basis for that interpretation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my view it was an example of the implementation of Article 26 of the 1992 Code of Discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But do you have any other examples such as this of General Gotovina taking disciplinary measures against a member of the 7th Guards Brigade, for example?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But we have documents we discussed dealing with one or two members of the 2nd Battalion of the 9 Guards Brigade who entered into the zone of separation and where again, in my view, in application of Article 26, it is General Gotovina who takes the disciplinary measure or who orders the disciplinary measure against these two members, even though the 9 Guards Brigade is not an organic unit of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So why doesn't General Gotovina issue a disciplinary measure in this instance of a traffic violation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Article 26 leaves the commander the freedom to decide whether he considers it a serious incident or not. If he considers it a serious incident, and, again, we have discussed the aims or the objectives of military discipline, a serious incident could also affect the behaviour of other soldiers, so in that case the commander has an interest in acting himself. If he doesn't consider this a serious incident, he can defer the matter to the establishment or the organic commander of the violator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, let's turn to D844, please. This is a document from the 4th of August. We can tell not by the top but at the stamp lines of when it was transmitted and received on the back of this page. It's, again, an order by General Lausic. You will note that he issues this order, skipping various persons in the chain of command and sends it directly to the 3rd Company of the 72nd MPs; the 4th Company, Sibenik, and the 6th Company, Dubrovnik telling them how they are to report matters, and if you look at the introduction he says: "With a view of the uniform contents of reports on tasks performance in the areas of responsibility, it says the report is to be submitted directly to the MP administration by using code system." If we turn the page please. Point 2: "Amongst the things they are to report, the status of public law and order in a zone of combat operations and in newly liberated areas, stating events when the MP had to act and results of intervention." Number 4: "The status of crime in liberated areas and in zones of combat operations. Number of crimes, crime reports filed, and escort of HV members who committed a crime." Number 6 is: "Search results of territory and facilities." 23 What is significant about the fact that General Lausic issues orders directly to the companies of the 72nd MP Battalion on the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we maybe see the first page again. This document is discussed on English page 215, part 2, of the report. I noticed -- I mean, the same issue as Mr. Misetic highlights, I found it unusual that the chief of the military police administration would issue an order directly to military police companies, because the normal command and control along professional and operational chain, would imply or would mean that he, that Lausic would send the order to the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, and I have not been able to find a plausible explanation for what appears to be a non-application of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at your report right now at page 215, subparagraph F. You just referenced that a report -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I think it is under 7, because it is 475 and not 474, last three digits, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You didn't note, though, that you found something unusual about this order.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not put that in writing in my report. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is there a reason you didn't put in writing that you found this order to be unusual?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because the only think I would be able to say is well, look this is unusual in my view, but I haven't been able to -- as I said to -- haven't been able to determine what the reason was for this, and I don't -- I didn't that the reader would have much benefit from me saying, Well, this is unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, does it, now as we're looking at the overall context of documents, do you think this is a factor to consider in evaluating your overall opinion about who had operational control over certain matters in the zone of the 72nd Military Police Battalion? Is this an important document in that regard?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- it is important in light of the aspect to whom are the military police units, and more specifically, the military police units of the Split Military District reporting. And whether they keep the commander of the Split Military District, or when we are talking about the military police units operating in the OGs, whether they keep the OGs informed of their activities and their observations. Now, it is correct that this document only refers to reporting to the military police administration. However, I would also like to draw your attention to the minutes or reporting that is included in P71, the operational diary, where we do notice that the commander or his representative of the military police in the Split Military District informs the operational commanders of their observations and the problems and their activities during the working meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, again, let's try to focus again. Okay? The issue here is the reporting on issues such as status of crime, number of crimes, crime reports filed, and escort of HV members who committed a crime, that information, according to this order, is supposed to go to the MP administration, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You did not find -- or did you find any written reports being submitted by the 72nd MP Battalion or Major Juric to General Gotovina on these topics?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen such documents being submitted during Operation Storm, but there are statistical reports included -- included in my report which were compiled by the military police on -- on these issues but they date from much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So in terms of when we're looking at the period of 4 August to, let's say, 30 August, these reports are being sent to the MP administration. Correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be sure about the end date, but indeed such reports -- I mean, reports on the activities of the military police units including information that is pointed out in -- in this document are indeed sent by the military police units of the Split Military District to the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have D732 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a report for the 9th of August by Major Juric. It goes to General Lausic. It does not go to the Split Military District even for information. This is his daily report for the 9th. He talks about the execution of MP tasks in OG North; appliances being seized; case of seizing items, seized at check-points anyway. Next page talks about someone having a tractor seized from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to, Mr. Registrar, Exhibit D733, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is Mr. Juric's report for the 10th of August. Again, it goes to Mr. Lausic directly. It's not copied to the Split Military District. He is again reporting on military police tasks carried out in OG North. "No violations of public law and order were registered in the observed period."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could go to Exhibit D734, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He is reporting on -- for example, 4th Company what check-points its holding. "We expect that members of the MUP will take over security in Kistanje. Check-points and security in Drnis remained unchanged." The 5th Company in Sinj, talks about their check-points, regular police duties. The 3rd Company in Benkovac talks about being engaged at nine check-points and control duty in beat duty sectors. Coordination meeting on 11th of August with the Obrovac police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He states that the Benkovac VP platoon can no longer secure the Krka monastery, and that police were informed of that. Securing the Glinica factory. If you go through this, number 4 says: "In the VP military police section perpetrators of crimes, misappropriation of property from liberated areas are being processed daily." Mr. Theunens, Mr. Juric is providing pretty specific details about what features are being secured how many check-points are in a particular location, what the status of crime processing is, et cetera, and he is only reporting it to Mr. Lausic. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document does not allow -- or these type of documents only allow to conclude that indeed Juric sends the information to Lausic but does not allow to conclude as to whether he shares information included in the report or a similar report with anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is your job, isn't it, Mr. Theunens? Why don't you tell us if you found such documents?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is correct that I have not come across documents by Major Juric to General Gotovina, but, again, I emphasise the importance of the presence of the commander of the military police of the Split Military District at the working meetings. As we can see from P71, written reporting is one way of reporting. There can also be oral reporting. When we look at the document that is now on the monitor, there is information included under number 2 provided by the -- it is listed as the 142nd Brigade, but it should be the 142nd Home Guard Regiment, indicating that the military police and the operational units or the combat units are in contact and exchange information. But, again, this document or these type of documents only allows to conclude that indeed information is being sent by Juric to -- to Lausic, and without further conclusions being able to be drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Theunens: Speaking generally now, wouldn't a neutral analyst in trying to determine who has certain responsibilities in a chain of command, wouldn't a neutral analyst first look at who is being -- who is issuing the orders to a specific unit, and who is filing written reports, written reports, to whom is that unit filing written reports? Wouldn't a neutral analyst first fundamentally start from that proposition and build his analysis from there, but isn't that the first place that a neutral analyst should look?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concept of neutral analyst is new to me, but I have explained my methodology and I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neutrality, of course, might be of great importance for an expert witness. You will understand that. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand the concept of neutrality as well as the concept of objectivity. I have explained the methodology. I have reviewed documents and drawn conclusions on these documents. If I were not neutral, I would certainly not have included -- I will rephrase that. There are many documents included in my report which are in the meanwhile Defence exhibits. I have drawn conclusions on groups of documents, these conclusions can be found in the executive summary. I also explain why I draw these conclusions. Now, whether somebody else would draw other conclusions from these documents is something I do not control. The conclusions I have drawn from the documents I reviewed are based on my training, my education, and my understanding of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I again asked you a specific question and with all due respect -- and again you're someone who works in the building so I will put this to you. I posed that question to you first as a specific question, but also because every answer thus far has to have a spin on it because you don't want to address the fundamental matter first, which is, let's deal with the issue first. I think you know full well, as someone who worked in the military, that the first step you would take to determine who a particular unit is subordinated to is to look to who is issuing orders to them and who is that unit reporting to. I don't think that is a difficult concept for you to agree with. Do you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree but it's a different question from what you asked earlier. Of course, one of the things you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You agree, and you say that question was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we start from that fundamental concept or principle and we agree on it, let's take it the next step, which is Major Juric neither receives an order from General Gotovina nor sends a report to General Gotovina on what he is doing. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the documents that I have reviewed, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would like to take you back to your direct examination and take you to the transcript for the 21st of November 2008. It is page -- beginning at page 12340, line 22, and it continues on to the next page. You said: "Your Honours, as explained earlier, the 73rd Military Police Battalion even though it is located in Split is not an organic unit of the Split Military District. It belongings normally to the navy. However, for operational reasons, the 73rd Military Police Battalion had been ordered to assist the 72nd Military Police Battalion, i.e., it becomes a unit of the Split Military District. And in order to facility command and control over these two units, a coordinator or -- yeah, a coordinator has been appointed, namely Major Juric." And here is the sentence: "This makes it easier both for the military police administration as well as for the command of the Split Military District to give instructions to the military police as they only have to speak to one person, i.e., Ivan Juric." Do you recall giving that testimony on direct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You say there that he is appointed in order to make it easier for, not only the military police administration, but the command of the Split Military District to give instructions to the military police as they only have to speak to one person, Ivan Juric. But you acknowledge, do you not, that there are no instructions from the Split Military District that ever went to Major Juric; right? And you have acknowledged this morning that Major Juric was subordinated to General Lausic and not General Gotovina. So I'm asking now to reconcile what you said today with what you said on Friday.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 65 ter 419 includes a document signed by the command of the 3rd Company of the 72nd Military Police Battalion showing that when that company is operating or participating in -- among other things, in combat tasks with units of OG Zadar, that Major Juric is there to facilitate relations between that company and OG Zadar. When I say "facilitate relations" I mean ensure a smooth implementation of command control, coordination, and related aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's put 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I may ask for your assistance, 65 ter 419 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then if you could use this document to please tell me how this document means that the Split Military District is facilitating command and control over these units by issuing instructions to Major Juric?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, am I wrong that 65 ter 419 has been mentioned before today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is not in evidence, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. He mentioned it today, I believe. I don't recall before today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I'm saying today. Before, today, but it is not in evidence if I'm -- my recollection is well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is why I think it is a good idea to bring it up and move it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that is already on the list provided by Mr. Waespi, so no additional exercise is needed to get it. Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Theunens, you're using this document to explain how the Split Military District gave instructions to the military police as they only have to speak to one person, i.e. -- I'm sorry, the command of the Split Military District gave instructions to the military police as they only have to speak to one person, Ivan Juric. So I would like you to point out to me the instructions in this document that are being issued by the Split Military District Command to Major Juric?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I addressed the role of Major Juric on Friday, I think that I used the term "if." So I don't see the transcript anymore here, but what I -- my recollection is, and also what I wanted to say is that if the military police administration or the Split Military District want to give instructions to the military police, it is easier if they only have to speak to one person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read to you literally what you said. After you had explained that it was for the purpose of facilitating command and control over the two units, that Major Juric was appointed, you said: "This makes it easier both for the military police administration, as well as for the command of the Split Military District to give instructions to the military police as they only have to speak to one person, i.e., Ivan Juric." That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you, Mr. President. In my view, that doesn't necessarily mean that the Split Military District issued instructions to Juric, yes or no. From the written documents I have reviewed and the documents I had access to, I haven't seen any document showing that the Split Military District Command issues instructions to Mr. Juric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well -- sorry, go ahead. I thought you were finished.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: 65 ter 419, the first page, shows the role -- is a document that gives information on the role of Major Ivan Juric in relation to his position between the 72nd Military Police Battalion and, as this document shows, the commander of OG Zadar, Colonel Fuzul.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, let's take this step by step. What you said on Friday, therefore was not based on any documents -- any analysis of documents that you had seen in this case, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was based on -- there's one order we discussed also today by General Lausic where he clarifies the role of Major Juric, stating that he is superior over the 72nd -- over the 73rd Military Police Battalion for issues related to the support of the 73rd to the 72nd Military Police Battalion. And I can find the correct phrasing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's okay, because I'm more particularly interested in the opinion that you gave that says: "It made it easier for the command of the Split Military District to give instructions to the military police as they only have to speak to one person, i.e., Ivan Juric." That opinion was not based on any document that you had seen. In fact, was contradicted by the documents you had seen. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to clarify, I said it makes -- which is an indeed a theoretical observation. It makes it easier to implement command and control. I didn't say "it made," because "it made" would indeed imply that I documents from the Split Military District Command or orders from the Split Military District Command to Major Juric, and I don't -- I don't have these documents. So there a little nuance in it, which I consider important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, since we go in such detail as far as the specific lines are concerned, I'd like, which I would have otherwise refrained of, put on the record that where you earlier said that this was the purpose for appointing Mr. Juric, that that's not what the text says. The first time you put this to the witness, you phrased it a little bit different from what we just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't know how I phrased it, Your Honour, but I believe I raid the entire answer that he gave in order to make it as specific as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you would wind up in the next two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The reason this issue is important to me is, in fact, what you said on Friday and what you now concede was the reality of how it actually unfolded, i.e., Mr. Juric reported -- received his orders from Mr. Lausic, reported to Mr. Lausic. You have no evidence that he received orders from General Gotovina or that he reported to General Gotovina. This, in fact, now violates the principle of unit of command, doesn't it, because now you have an actor in the field in Mr. Juric who is receiving instructions on day to day matters from Mr. Lausic and also implementing his own orders in the field on day to day matters, while at the same time you say that General Gotovina also is exercising command over day-to-day matters in the zone of the 72nd MP Battalion. Does that note violate the principle of unity of command?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Because we would have to analyse the specific instructions Generals Lausic and Gotovina are giving to -- to Juric or to the military police of the Split Military District in general, and then see whether they fall under the professional line or the operational line, and then we could draw conclusions as to the principle of unity of command and control is being violated or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We're going into a break now, so during the break, I'm going to follow up on that question. And I would ask you during the break to then breakdown further for me what tasks fall under the professional line, your word, that would have been something that Major Juric was taking care of and what tasks fell under the operational line, which would have been tasks that General Gotovina would have been issuing orders on. You will have time on the break to consider your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think it's a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a break until ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to check, Mr. Waespi, is 65 ter 4600 on your list as well, because that was another exhibit mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Not yet, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And because we have to -- specific exhibits to which reference is made, we should receive them in evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, let me repeat --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens let me repeat now and follow up on your last response. What were the quote/unquote "professional line tasks" that Mr. Juric was dealing with, and what were the quote/unquote "operational tasks" that General Gotovina was dealing with?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports we have seen, I mean, the reports complied by Mr. Juric and which he sent to General Lausic referred to the implementation of the tasks by the military police, whereby it is not always clear to determine who has imposed these tasks. The fact that he informs General Lausic about the implementation of a particular task doesn't have to mean at it has been imposed by Lausic, because I recall that some of these reports also address the participation in combat operations by units of the Split Military District military police. In general terms, the tasks along the professional line are, for example, the ones included in P881, i.e., the establishment of the -- of a permanent military police presence in the recently recaptured area. There's also tasks in relation to actually the follow-up order from the meeting between Messrs. Jarnjak and Susak involving Moric and Lausic, and I believe that is D47, where specific tasks are given as to how refugees or prisoners of war are to be escorted and also how check-points are to be established. There is also -- it is not D47. I will find the correct reference. Because D47 is not a document. D47 actually -- is an order by General Lausic for the reduction of combat readiness in the military police units, whereby in paragraph 14 of that order, D47, General Lausic confirms that the military police is subordinated to the most senior HV commander in the zone of responsibility and sent the daily report to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, if I could interrupt you, because I want to get back to the question. Your answer is: "We have reports about tasks that Mr. Juric was dealing with, but it is not always clear to determine who imposed these tasks?" Now it is clear that have you no evidence that you have seen that General Gotovina was imposing those tasks upon Mr. Juric, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have not answered the second part of the previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, because we go off on D47 and what is in D47, et cetera, and I'm trying to you back to concentrate on my question. Let answer the first part of the question, which is: Major Juric is doing certain tasks. What we know is that have you not seen any evidence that General Gotovina was issuing orders to Mr. Juric concerning what tasks he should undertake. I think we have established that, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can we also, by means of your review of the documents that and the fact that you indicated that Mr. Juric was subordinated to General Lausic, would your logical conclusion be that the tasks he is implementing, he is implementing pursuant to orders of his superior, General Lausic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit -- I mean, you mentioned the cart and the horse earlier. We can conclude that if General Lausic issues him -- gives him a task that he implements it. But the fact that he carries out a task does not necessarily mean that it comes from General Lausic, even though it is General Lausic who sends Juric to the zone of responsibility of the Split Military District, and even though General Lausic establishes the general taskings or the role of Major Juric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Completely agree, Mr. Theunens, because, as we know, every commander then has to make -- or every officer in the chain then has to implement his tasks by making his own decisions and issuing his own orders to his subordinates. That is understood. But my question is, Mr. Juric is acting on the basis of orders that he has received from his superior, Mr. Lausic, on what his tasks are. How he is going to implement them, et cetera, that's something for Mr. Juric to determine as he -- as matters transpire in the field. Do you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, based on the documents I was able -- I had access to and I could review.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That leads me now to the next question, which is: What types of tasks, according to your review of the documents, is Mr. Juric dealing with? And I will -- for example, if we can look at D732 to make things a bit -- actually, hold on before we get there. D734. Now, in this report by Major Juric, he is reporting back to Mr. Lausic. For example, securing facilities -- sorry, check-points is point 1. "The 4th OVP company Sibenik is no longer holding the check-points at certain locations. We expect that members of the MUP will take over security in Kistanje during the day. The check-points and security in Drnis remain unchanged." Do you agree with me that one of the tasks that Major Juric was dealing was check-points in the newly liberated territories in the zone of responsibility of the 72nd Military Police and the 73rd Military Police?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And I just want to clarify that, based on the documents I reviewed, the manning or the organising of check-points was ordered both -- I mean, in general terms, by the military police administration through -- from General Lausic to Major Juric, as well as by the operational commanders, and we have in that context, for example, we discussed P1129.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: P1129, is that the order of General Ademi?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can show it. It is signed by Brigadier Ademi or General Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But that's to establish a check-point on the Strmica Knin, Gracac cross-road. Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get into that a little bit later on my cross-examination. As a general matter, Mr. Lausic [sic], would you agree with me that the command of the Split Military District is issuing orders for check-points, it is in the context of movement of troops or securing convoys, those types of matters. Let's first speak generally.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we would be -- we would benefit from showing -- if we want to go into the P1129 or the matters addressed in P1129, it would be helpful to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to show you the entire context of P1129, and we're going get into why that check-point was established, so I don't want to take a half an hour to do that right now. Putting that document aside and looking at the all the documents as a whole which you have done, do you agree with me that when the Military District establishes a check-point -- and let me stop and tell what you my distinction is here. Mr. Juric is establishing check-points pursuant to the agreement with MUP in terms of providing general security in the area; whereas, when Brigadier Ademi or General Gotovina issue an order, it is generally in the context of a combat zone and securing entry and exit into a combat zone or a military escort of -- of troop movements or something in that context, generally speaking. Let's put aside the exceptions to the rules. Generally speaking, that is what those orders relate to, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to make such a distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The particular order -- that instructs the addresses to establish a check-point also determines what the role is of the check-point, and the -- the mean, the orders issued by General Gotovina or Brigadier Ademi, in my view, also deal with what you describe as a military police check-point or a purely military police task, even though in both cases, be it military police administration or General Gotovina or Ademi, the military police of the Split Military District is ordered to establish a check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: First we'll go off on this digression now if you want to talk about that order, I believe it is the 18th of August. But first Major Juric is setting up check-points pursuant to the agreement with MUP, wouldn't you agree, on the joint military police MUP check-points? Isn't that what is really is being talked about here?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially I agree with you. At the start of Operation Storm, when the military police follows the combat units and then establishes check-points to prevent, for example, civilians from entering or also to -- in the framework of securing the area, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now -- and those check-points and that control is being commanded by Major Juric in the field as one of his tasks. Correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to draw that conclusion. I mean, the military police reports, i.e., the reports I have seen from -- for example General Lausic, where he informs the addressees of his report about the activity of the military police, it is not always clear who actually had ordered what at that very moment. He talks about the activities of military police manning check-points, escorting prisoners of war, receiving the prisoners of war and other military police tasks, including also participating in combat tasks. But as I mentioned, based on my understanding of these reports, it is not always clear who has imposed or issued that particular task to the military police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's take it to the next step. If is not clear to you, then let's work this way. Reports about where check-points are established in towns like Sibenik, Benkovac, Kistanje, Drnis, et cetera, speaking now about the wider liberated territory, from everything you have seen, those reports about check-points go to the military police administration in Zagreb, right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you have not seen any document where a report is being sent to General Gotovina that says, There are the check-points here in Drnis that have been set up with MUP and Sibenik. They have been et up at these locations in Benkovac. They have been set up in these locations, correct? There is no such report to General Gotovina about specific check-points in the wider -- in the wider area.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Applying -- I mean, following military system of command and control and also the chain of command, I do not rule out that such reports could have been sent to Gotovina, but I haven't seen any. But it would make more sense that there is direct cooperation and coordination between the operational commander in the area, at the lowest level, that would be battalion level, for example, if we talk about a -- check-points. The military police, together with the civilian police is to establish check-points in Benkovac. That they notify the operational commander of the existence or the intention to establish such check-points. When I say "they," to the military police, i.e., Juric. I would expect him to coordinate with the operational commander in the area to state -- to determine where the check-points should be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I -- I absolutely respect your assessment of what you would expect in such situations. I'm more interested, however, in what you found.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And correct me if I'm wrong, what you found was that reports about check-points and where they're being set up were not going to the Split Military District Command, right? That is actually what you found, even if it is against what you would expect to find?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about check-points established or manned by the military and civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And their exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then when they are being moved, or example, Juric in this report talks about the military police is no longer at certain check-points but is at a different check-point now, et cetera, as things transpired on a day to day basis. This type of information about these joint check-points was not being send to the Split Military District Command, right, as far as you know from the documents?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the documents I have reviewed, I have not come across a document that indicates that indeed such information was sent to the Split Military District Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, a simple no would have been exactly the same answer, isn't it? In view of the questions which already includes all the reservations, Mr. Misetic, by now, expects you to make. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, based -- we can only work on the evidence that's before us, whether it is us in the courtroom or you as an expert witness, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you agree with me that with respect to the evidence that is before you, the conclusion that you would draw, based on the evidence that is before you, is that the issue of the joint check-points their implementation, locations, when they would be changed, those types of questions, were under the command of Major Juric, and his line was to General Lausic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have answered the question already, whereby I stated that -- and this is also referred to on page 213 in my report, using P915 that indeed initially it is the military police who decide about the establishment of the check-points, when -- I mean, during the advance of the HV units. As to what happens later, especially after Storm, in my view, the reports, both by Lausic -- by Juric as well by Lausic do not always allow to conclude who ordered to establish the check-point where. There is no doubt that some check-points or that the check-points were established following orders by the military police administration, but, again, as the reports do not clearly indicate who ordered what, I cannot draw a -- an overall conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But to follow up on that, there's also the fact that -- you said you can't conclude, but you also -- even after Operation Storm, as events transpired, you didn't find an order from General Gotovina at any time regarding joint MUP military police check-points, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not come across such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's on the screen now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: For example, this is it dated 11 August, and it talks about the third paragraph : "The Benkovac platoon of the 3rd military police Company Zadar is engaged at nine check-points ... on 11 August 1995 a coordination meeting was held with the members of the Obrovac police station." That would be MUP police, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "And we informed them about our evaluation of public law and order situation in that municipality and that at 0600 hours on that day the Benkovac VP platoon could no longer secure the Krka monastery." Then it goes on. Now my question is it is it also a fact that MUP and the military police were coordinating their activities on the ground. Correct? We agree that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Or I should say attempting as best they could to coordinate their activities. And the reports by joint meetings about what they were doing to coordinate, at least through August 11 in this report, were again being sent through major Juric to General Lausic, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That is that what document shows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you did not find any reports about the results of joint coordination meetings between MUP and the military police being sent to the Split Military District Command, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is an document from General Lausic which he sends to the military police units all over Croatia following a meeting he has had with Mr. Moric, where the -- the difficulties in -- in coordination of the tasks between civilian police and military police are addressed, and to my recollection, that document is also being sent to -- sent info to the Military District Commanders and this is P877, dated the 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, maybe I should have been more precise. I'm not referring to General Lausic at his level, then sending things for information to the Split Military District. I'm talking about these subordinate military police personnel that in the field are having these coordination meetings with the MUP. These subordinate personnel in the field are reporting the results of their coordination activities to Mr. Lausic through Major Juric, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We have a example on the screen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in your review of the OTP documents, you do not find a report where subordinate -- subordinate military police in the 72nd MPs were sending reports of coordination meetings with the MUP to the Split Military District command, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Number 4, status of crime, processing of crime. In terms of the work of the crime police of the military police on a daily basis, those reports were being sent to the military police administration on a daily basis, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were regularly sent. I'm not sure anymore whether these were compiled on a daily basis, but indeed there was a procedure to inform the military police administration of this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the regular reports of the crime police in the 72nd MP were not sent to the Split Military District Command, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only answer based on the documents I have reviewed, and indeed, I have not seen such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the -- so let's stop here and go back to the distinction you made before the break, which is Major Juric is dealing with what you call tasks in the professional line, and General Gotovina dealing with tasks in the operational line. If we see that -- I'm Major Juric is dealing with the issue of these joint check-points with the MUP, if we see that Major Juric is dealing with the issue of crime processing in the zone of the 72nd of MUP, are those, in fact, then tasks that fall within the professional line of the military police?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we -- when you mean "crime processing," do you also mean actually to -- do note -- or to observe that a crime has happened and then to start investigation afterwards, or do you only mean by that the -- the investigative activities? Once the military police has been notified of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Once it has been notified of a crime. So the regular -- what was in Article 10 -- part of regular duties to investigate and process crime, and if necessary, bring a criminal complaint, and all the things you would expect a military police crime unit to do.
